title: Module 1 · Lesson 2 — The agent loop and its control policies

lines: Welcome to Module One, Lesson Two: the agent loop and its control policies.
Every agent, in every framework, runs the same loop.
Picture TripWise, a travel startup whose agent books trips overnight.
One morning, the team wakes up to an eighteen-hundred-dollar bill.

say.0: Picture Trip Wise, a travel startup whose agent books trips overnight.

lines: A flight-search tool had returned the same error since midnight.
The agent kept calling it, and nothing told it to stop.
Start with the loop: perceive, reason, act, observe.
Gather the state, let the model pick a step, run the tool, and append the result.
Notice that the model only proposes a tool name and arguments.
Your runtime checks the call and runs it, so every security control lives in code.
When a tool fails, don't crash: return the error as an observation, so the model can re-plan.
But bound the retries, because the same failing call three times means escalate.
A complete design names five control policies.
Termination, tool exposure, state management, error handling, and escalation.
Termination says when the loop stops, and tool exposure says which tools the model sees.
State management decides what carries forward.
Error handling chooses to retry, fall back, or degrade gracefully.
Escalation hands over to a human, say after repeated failure or before an irreversible action.
TripWise had no termination policy, and budgets are not optional.
Every loop needs a step cap, a cost cap, and a timeout, checked before each model call.

say.0: Trip Wise had no termination policy, and budgets are not optional.

lines: Hitting a cap must fire an alert, never fail silently.
Add loop detection for repeated identical calls, and require each iteration to change the state.
Then a second problem: on long trips, the agent forgot its earlier bookings.
A raw message list collapses by step fifty, as the context window fills.
The fix is structured state: goal, plan, findings, and completed steps as typed fields.
Summarise older turns, and store big tool outputs by reference.
On the exam, an agent that works on short tasks but degrades on long ones needs context management.
It's not a bigger model or more retries, so read on for the full lesson.
